I attribute the fault less due to the medium and setting, and more due to its popularity.

[ORGANIZATION] is popular. That means many many stories and works are being made in that style. But great and good authors aren’t common. So that just results in a large number of mediocre writers all copy pasting the same character and setting archetypes over and over again. 

This is a big reason for [ORGANIZATION]’s genericness. It’s borrowing and using concepts that an audience is already familiar with as the foundation of its setting in order to save effort on establishing it. Because so many writers are using the same concepts without bothering to expand upon them, it leads to things all feeling extremely similar. 

That’s why there’s always self-insert males being tasked by godly beings and gifted grand powers off having adventures to defeat some enigmatic and undefined evil force.

Exceptions do exist. [PERSON] uses the exact setup, but outright ignores it in favor of pure slapstick comedy and character interaction (everyone loves the gang, nobody cares about the demon lord). Re Zero and Cautious Hero also use the premise, but have their main protagonists be terrible people that nobody can self-insert as. [ORGANIZATION] and [PERSON] set the main goals as something completely different, but this leaves them falling back into generic once those goals are fulfilled.
